AI Summary

Three papers this cycle land squarely on lab systems. Plowman & Kassiotis assembled an NMD-extended transcriptome of roughly 217,000 transcripts (~80% unannotated) from long-read sequencing after nonsense-mediated decay inhibition, and found NMD-regulated transcripts enriched for TE exonization — specifically LTR and LINE integrations entering annotated genes as alternative isoforms. The TEs that NMD silences are evolutionarily younger, more diverged, carry younger and less conserved splice sites, and more often encode functionally distinct protein isoforms; primate-specific Alu-exonizing isoforms of DDX49, NEIL3 and SETDB1 yield stable proteins with distinct activities. This is the IFNAR2 decoy-receptor logic generalized into a rule: TE exonization supplies the raw isoform diversity, and NMD sets how much of that reservoir survives to be translated. The SETDB1 hit is pointed, since an Alu-exonized isoform of an H3K9 methyltransferase sits inside the very silencing machinery that restrains TE derepression. Englander et al. is the second must-read: long-read RNA sequencing of primary human lung adenocarcinomas recovered more than 149,000 full-length mRNA isoforms, over half of them unannotated, with many falling in immune-related genes and concentrated in the type I interferon response pathway — and intron retention in STAT2 regulates its function and tracks with immunotherapy response. Third, Calendo et al. released TEDEdb, a uniform reanalysis of over 7,000 RNA-seq samples spanning 220 cancer cell lines and 700 drug treatments, which confirms DNMT and HDAC inhibitors as TE inducers and adds CDK and topoisomerase inhibitors as non-epigenetic drugs that drive TE-derived expression with a viral-mimicry transcriptional signature.

Read together, those three describe one pipeline and this digest fills in its middle. Non-canonical transcript architecture is the recurring theme: Buen Abad Najar et al. introduce Torino, which factorizes RNA-seq coverage directly rather than relying on transcript annotations, and recover exactly the event classes that annotation-dependent and junction-based tools miss — intron retention, cryptic splicing and alternative polyadenylation — mapping thousands of coverage-pattern QTLs that colocalize with disease risk loci, including an Alzheimer's risk variant increasing intron retention in KNOP1. That is the right tool shape for intronic-TE-driven premature termination and alternative TSS usage, where the causal isoform is by definition absent from the reference. On the epitranscriptomic side, Kwon et al. mapped m6A in lncRNAs at single-base resolution and found methylation distributed broadly along lncRNAs rather than clustered as in mRNAs, attributing the difference partly to TE-derived sequence shaping DRACH motif availability and local RNA structure, with m6A also bearing on lncRNA polyadenylation. TE sequence content is therefore not just a substrate for exonization but a determinant of where the m6A machinery deposits marks — directly relevant to how METTL3/METTL14 inhibition changes TE exonization. Di Giorgio et al. attack the adjacent question in macrophages, using Nanopore direct RNA sequencing in METTL3- and ADAR1-deficient RAW cells to resolve m6A and A-to-I co-occurrence on single molecules; since A-to-I editing concentrates in SINEs and introns whose duplexes would otherwise trip MDA5, this is the TE-dsRNA-sensing axis read at molecular resolution.

The immunity and cancer papers converge on how tumors and cells throttle nucleic-acid sensing, which is the output side of viral mimicry. Gao et al. report that CREBBP loss epigenetically silences both STING and MHC-I in small cell lung cancer — a chromatin lesion that simultaneously removes the sensor and the presentation machinery, and the mirror image of the H3K9 methyltransferase pathways whose disruption releases TE-derived dsRNA. Zhang et al. add a post-translational brake: hexokinase-2 dissociates from mitochondria under ROS, binds STING, and blocks its oligomerization and Golgi translocation independently of glycolytic activity. Saha et al. push the pathway the other way in colon cancer, where serine depletion or serine palmitoyltransferase mutation raises deoxysphingolipids, releases mitochondrial DNA, and activates cGAS-STING with immune infiltration and tumor suppression. Two cautions sit alongside: Dushimyineza et al. show chromosome-derived eccDNA produces cGAS-dependent STING accumulation without Ser366 phosphorylation or cytokine output, so STING protein levels are not a readout of STING signaling — worth remembering when scoring TE-derepression experiments. On enhancer logic, Leão et al. show NF-κB p65 Ser276 phosphorylation recruits CBP/p300 and licenses latent enhancer engagement, selecting which inflammatory genes fire from identical upstream signaling. Latent, signal-dependent enhancers are the functional class MER41 and LTR10 elements occupy, so a phospho-mark that gates latent enhancer activation is a candidate control point for ERV-derived enhancers under MAPK/AP1 and interferon input.

On the variation-and-methods side, Kathail et al. review sequence-to-activity models and genomic language models for noncoding variant effect prediction, and are explicit about which ground-truth datasets make these models trustworthy and in which settings they are not — directly applicable to scoring polymorphic TE insertions and VNTRs as regulatory variation. Das et al. supply the matching experimental readout with UDI-UMI-STARR-seq over 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 candidate enhancers, paired with CRISPR knockouts of six transcription factors and a deep learning model that recovers cooperative motif syntax and flanking sequence context. Comparative work rounds it out: Termignoni-Garcia et al. provide the first direct avian evidence of genome shock, with Swainson's thrush hybrids showing elevated TE proportions, TE expression and chromatin accessibility relative to parental lineages, localized to regulatory regions and linked to retinoic acid receptor signaling — hybridization as a natural experiment in TE derepression and its regulatory consequences. Coverage this cycle was complete: 16 of 20 journals returned RSS and the bioRxiv scan finished all 3,325 records, so the slate reflects the full fortnight.
